problem.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problem.prompt: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. The algorithm's time complexity must be better than O(N log N), where N is the array's size.
requirements: Return the k most frequent elements in any order.
Time complexity must be strictly better than O(N log N).
Handle negative numbers and arrays with all identical elements.
k is always valid (1 <= k <= number of unique elements).
constraints: k is in the range [1, the number of unique elements in the array].
It is guaranteed that the answer is unique.

stages.learnerPrompt: Why does full sorting take O(N log N)? What approaches avoid full sorting? Compare min-heap vs bucket sort.

referenceMaterial.summary: First pass: frequency map takes O(N) time and O(U) space where U is unique elements. Full sort on frequencies is O(U log U). Min-heap of size k is O(N log k). Bucket sort where index represents frequency is O(N) linear time.
tradeOffs: Min-heap: O(N log k) time, O(N) space. Works on streaming data where total size N is unknown ahead of time.
Bucket sort: O(N) time, O(N) space. Requires finite bounded frequency space (max frequency is N).

stages.learnerPrompt: Write your approach. How will you store element counts? How will you extract the top k efficiently?
Review both Min-Heap and Bucket Sort reference solutions.

referenceMaterial.summary: Bucket Sort approach delivers optimal O(N) time complexity.
approachSteps: 1. Count occurrences of each number using a HashMap: freqMap[num] = count.
2. Create an array of buckets of size N+1, where bucket[i] holds numbers that appear i times.
3. Populate buckets: iterate through freqMap and append num to bucket[freqMap[num]].
4. Iterate from bucket[N] down to bucket[0], collecting numbers into result array until result.length === k.
alternatives: Quickselect: partition elements based on frequency until pivot is at index N-k. Average O(N), worst-case O(N^2).
Min-Heap of size k: push [freq, num]; if heap.size > k, pop minimum. O(N log k).

stages.learnerPrompt: When would you choose a Min-Heap over Bucket Sort in real production systems?

tradeOffs: Streaming input: In a live telemetry stream (e.g., top trending search queries), N is infinite. Bucket sort requires an end boundary. A Min-Heap or Count-Min Sketch operates continuously on unbounded streams.
Memory locality: Bucket sort creates an array of lists, causing memory fragmentation if U is sparse.

stages.learnerPrompt: Scale challenge: The input contains 10 billion search queries per day across 500 servers. How do you find the global Top K queries without sending all queries to a single machine?

failureModes: Single machine memory exhaustion: 10 billion queries cannot fit in RAM for a full HashMap count.
Distributed MapReduce / Spark: Map step computes local counts per partition; Shuffle partitions by query hash; Reduce aggregates global counts; final stage runs Top-K heap per reducer.
Probabilistic streaming (Heavy Hitters): Use Count-Min Sketch + Min-Heap (Space-Saving algorithm) on each edge node, then merge sketches at the aggregator with bounded error guarantees.

stages.learnerPrompt: Follow-up: What if k = 10,000 and queries arrive with timestamps, and we need the Top K queries within the last 15-minute sliding window?

approachSteps: 2. Compute Top-K sketch per minute bucket.
3. On window shift, drop the oldest bucket and sum counts from the remaining 14 buckets plus active bucket.
4. Query time: merge 15 bucket sketches and extract top K.
tradeOffs: Bucket granularity: 1-minute buckets give maximum 1-minute lag on eviction at low overhead. 1-second buckets increase precision at 60x memory cost.
